newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris says U.S. strikes on Iraq unjustified.
newsitem.headline: Paris says U.S. strikes on Iraq unjustified.

text.p: Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said on Sunday France had failed to back the U.S missile attacks against Iraq last week because Paris believed they were unjustified and it had not been sufficiently consulted.

"We are natural friends of the Americans but that does not prevent us from having our own views once in a while," De Charette told Radio Europe One from the Irish town of Tralee, where he was attending a European Union foreign ministers' meeting.
"We believe that on the subject (Iraqi moves against Kurdish opponents), there was no justification for a generalised bombing of Iraq," he said.
Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz later called on Paris to withdraw from U.S.-led surveillance operations over Iraq.
In a television interview, Aziz paid tribute to the French position and said Paris should reconsider its cooperation with the United States over Iraq.

"I would like to tell (French President) Jacques Chirac that I have great respect for him and his nation and that we greatly appreciate the position taken by France in favour of justice and legality, in a word, in favour of Iraq," Aziz said in an interview recorded in Baghdad by TF-1 television.

"We would like to have better relations with France like those we had in the past, but please reconsider your position concerning your participation in (flights over the) exclusion zones because you are contributing to violate Iraq's sovreignty and threatening our national security," he said.
De Charette said in his interview that Washington should have consulted France further before taking its actions inside Iraq.

"We do not believe that the movement of Iraqi troops inside Iraq alongside a Kurdish faction justified such a response. We believe the initiatives taken by the United States could have warranted more consultations with us on the subject," De Charette said.
Asked if Paris condemned the U.S. action, he replied: "Let's not use big words. There is a difference in analysis between the United States and us on the subject."
France's decision to refrain from approving the two U.S. cruise missile raids on Iraq, caused the most serious rift in the Gulf War coalition that forced Iraqi troops out of Kuwait in 1991.

France partially suspended participation in patrolling of Iraq's skies but resumed the flights later, although not beyond the 32nd parallel, to police an enlarged no-fly zone declared by U.S. President Bill Clinton.
But De Charette said he had particularly warm talks with U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher when he visited Paris on Thursday to discuss the issue.
